reference.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology / palliative care guidelines
clinicalPearls: Falls in older adults are usually multifactorial, and each additional risk factor further increases the likelihood of falling
A single fall warrants a gait and balance assessment, while recurrent falls or a fall with injury warrant a full multifactorial evaluation
Key contributors include muscle weakness, gait and balance disorders, visual impairment, cognitive impairment, environmental hazards, and culprit medications
Psychoactive drugs, antihypertensives, and drugs causing orthostatic hypotension are among the most modifiable medication-related risks
Always ask about loss of consciousness; syncopal falls point toward cardiac or neurological causes and require separate evaluation
Fear of falling is common after a fall and can itself cause activity restriction, deconditioning, and further falls
Multicomponent interventions, particularly progressive strength and balance exercise, are the most effective evidence-based prevention strategy
Vitamin D repletion in deficient individuals, home hazard modification, and correcting visual and footwear problems reduce fall risk
Screen for and manage osteoporosis, since the clinical consequence of falls is largely determined by fracture risk
reference.pathophysiology: Safe mobility depends on the integration of sensory input (vision, vestibular function, proprioception), central processing, and effector musculoskeletal responses. Ageing degrades each of these: sensory acuity declines, reaction times lengthen, postural reflexes slow, and sarcopenia reduces the strength needed for recovery. Superimposed disease (neurodegenerative disorders, arthritis, cardiovascular instability), medications, and environmental hazards further erode the margin of safety, so that balance perturbations that a younger person would correct instead result in a fall.
additionalDifferentials: Syncope from cardiac arrhythmia, structural heart disease, or vasovagal cause
Vertigo from vestibular disease including benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Mechanical or purely accidental trips related to environment
additionalInvestigations: Multifactorial falls assessment including gait, balance, and lower-limb strength testing
Orthostatic blood pressure measurement (lying and standing)
Medication review focused on psychoactive and hypotensive agents
Cardiac evaluation (ECG and further testing) when syncope is suspected
Bone health assessment including fracture risk and consideration of DXA
redFlags: Fall with head injury, especially on anticoagulants, raising concern for intracranial haemorrhage
Fall causing fracture or significant soft-tissue injury
Fall associated with loss of consciousness or suspected cardiac syncope
Long lie on the floor after a fall, with risk of rhabdomyolysis, pressure injury, hypothermia, and dehydration
New focal neurological signs suggesting stroke
reference.prognosis: Falls are a leading cause of injury, disability, and loss of independence in older people. A fall with fracture, particularly hip fracture, carries substantial morbidity and elevated one-year mortality. Recurrent falls predict functional decline and institutionalisation, but structured multifactorial intervention meaningfully reduces future falls in many patients.
pitfalls: Treating a fall as a simple mechanical accident and not searching for contributing medical causes
Overlooking orthostatic hypotension and culprit medications
Failing to distinguish a syncopal fall from a mechanical one
Ignoring bone health so that fracture risk is left unaddressed
Neglecting fear of falling and the resulting deconditioning spiral
